Bus 166
BUS 166 here. On your left— the church that named a district. Novena: once a weekly devotion from 1949, before that, simply the ninth milestone, and before that, a cemetery. Names shift; the ground endures. What does it mean to belong? You’re part of this moving story too. Let’s listen for the quiet between the noises, and see what rises to meet us.

Myna 1
Eh, we are in Novena already. Do You know why they call it that? Because of the weekly devotion from 1949.

Myna 2
Devotion ah? My grandmother say last time people just used to call this the "Ninth Milestone." Very ulu then.

Myna 1
Ulu only? Even earlier, it was a cemetery. First the dead, then the church, then the mall. The ground stays, but the humans just keep changing the name labels.

Bus 166
Passenger of Time. Here ends our journey—for now. We have crossed the island together, through places that have changed, places that are changing, and places that may soon exist only in memory. I have carried you as far as I can. But the journey does not end when you leave the bus. Take with you what you have heard. Look again at the roads, the trees, the birds, the spaces between buildings. The archive is not only behind us, It is being made every day. And perhaps, somewhere along the way, you have left something in it too. This is Bus 166. Thank you for travelling with me. Please take your belongings, and your memories, with you.

The Reclaimed Archive

The Reclaimed Archive
December 2013. Sakthivel Kumarvelu, A migrant worker struck and killed by a bus on Racecourse Road. Grief turned to fury, and Singapore saw its first riot in decades. Beneath that night lay deeper questions: How do migrant workers live? How are they seen? How do their rights matter? About 400 people took to the streets of the commercial district known as Little India, after Sakthivel Kumarvelu, an Indian construction worker was hit and killed by a bus.

Bus 166
It wasn’t my line. But buses are siblings— all cut from rubber, steel, and routes someone else designs. That night, they flipped one of us over. Set it on fire. Not out of hatred for a vehicle— but because pain needs a surface to strike against. I remember the heat even even if I wasn’t there. Every bus does. We carry people. We witness lives. Sometimes we carry the weight of what the city refuses to speak.
